people.name: Herwart Holland-Moritz
people.roles: hacker · journalist · Chaos Computer Club co-founder

keyWork.title: The Btx hack (with Steffen Wernéry), exposing the Bundespost's Bildschirmtext service

people.contribution: Holland was one of five Hamburg media activists who, in a notice in the Berlin newspaper taz on 1 September 1981, invited 'Komputerfrieks' to the 12 September 1981 meeting that the Chaos Computer Club counts as its informal founding. In November 1984 he and Steffen Wernéry used a Hamburger Sparkasse login to run up DM 134,634.88 on a CCC page in the Bundespost's Btx system, then went public to show the service was insecure. He lectured for years on people caught between media technology and surveillance, and died on 29 July 2001.

people.contribution: Barlow, a Wyoming rancher and Grateful Dead lyricist who met the 'electronic frontier' on the WELL, co-founded the Electronic Frontier Foundation with Mitch Kapor and John Gilmore in 1990 after the Secret Service raid on Steve Jackson Games. On 8 February 1996, the day the US Telecommunications Act (with its Communications Decency Act) became law, he wrote in Davos 'A Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace', rejecting government sovereignty over the online world. people.name: Richard M. Stallman
people.roles: programmer · founder of GNU and the Free Software Foundation
people.place: MIT Artificial Intelligence Lab, Cambridge, Massachusetts

keyWork.title: The GNU Project announcement ('Free Unix!') and the Free Software Definition

people.contribution: On 27 September 1983 Stallman, then at MIT's Artificial Intelligence Lab, announced GNU, a Unix-compatible system he would give away free, and went on to found the Free Software Foundation. His free-software definition makes user control of software a moral question: users should be free to run, copy, distribute, study, change and improve programs. After the Snowden disclosures he argued in Wired (October 2013) that general surveillance had reached a level incompatible with human rights. He resigned as FSF president on 16 September 2019 amid controversy and returned to its board in 2021, a decision the board acknowledged some found troubling.

people.name: Cory Doctorow

keyWork.title: Privacy Without Monopoly: Data Protection and Interoperability (EFF white paper, with Bennett Cyphers)

people.contribution: Toronto-born Doctorow, a former European director of the Electronic Frontier Foundation and co-founder of the UK's Open Rights Group, writes fiction and non-fiction about surveillance, including the young-adult novel Little Brother and the book How to Destroy Surveillance Capitalism. With EFF technologist Bennett Cyphers he co-wrote the February 2021 white paper Privacy Without Monopoly, which argues that big platforms' privacy failures and their market power are linked. It proposed mandates for data portability, back-end interoperability and 'delegability' — letting users' own software act on platforms for them.

people.name: Aaron Swartz

keyWork.title: DeadDrop, the anonymous document-submission system later renamed SecureDrop (with Kevin Poulsen)

people.contribution: Swartz, one of the three coders who sold Reddit to Condé Nast in 2006 and an activist for open information, built tools for anonymous publishing: in October 2008 he released a tor2web proxy so that ordinary browsers could reach sites hidden on Tor. people.name: Kevin Poulsen

people.contribution: In the late 1980s and early 1990s Poulsen was a notorious hacker: a 1993 federal indictment accused him of seizing control of the incoming phone lines of Los Angeles radio stations, by hacking Pacific Bell's computers, to win their contests, and of setting up his own wiretaps. After Swartz's death he launched it as Strongbox at The New Yorker in May 2013 and handed it to the Freedom of the Press Foundation, which renamed it SecureDrop, in October 2013.

events.title: Kapor and Barlow announce the Electronic Frontier Foundation
events.summary: After a 1 March 1990 Secret Service raid on Steve Jackson Games in Austin, Texas, in which the company's bulletin-board e-mail was accessed and deleted, Mitch Kapor, John Perry Barlow and John Gilmore formed an organisation for civil liberties raised by new technologies. Kapor and Barlow announced the Electronic Frontier Foundation in Washington on 10 July 1990, with a founding paper asking whether 'the history of one's personal business affairs' could properly belong to someone else. The lawsuit EFF announced at its launch, for Steve Jackson Games, ended in a 1993 federal ruling that the seizure of users' stored e-mail violated the Electronic Communications Privacy Act. EFF calls it the first time a court held that e-mail deserves at least as much protection as telephone calls.
events.significance: Created an advocacy organisation built specifically to argue for privacy and speech rights inside networks, and framed personal data as something that might belong to the person.

sources.note: --check FOUND 2026-09-23. Also FOUND: 'The judge did not find that Secret Service agents had "intercepted" the electronic communications'. The decision was announced 12 March 1993 by Judge Sam Sparks. This is the actual holding behind the summary's reworded sentence.

sources.title: John Perry Barlow, 'A Not Terribly Brief History of the Electronic Frontier Foundation'
sources.quote: We announced the formation of the Electronic Frontier Foundation at the National Press Club on July 10.
sources.note: --check FOUND 2026-09-23; page dated 'Thursday, November 8, 1990'. Also FOUND: 'One of our first official acts had been to grant that organization $275,000 for a project on computing and civil liberties.' (the organisation is CPSR) and 'the government was forced to abandon its case against Neidorf after 4 days in Chicago's Federal Court.' The office address '155 Second St. Cambridge, MA 02141' is on the same page.

events.locationNote: Announcement site (National Press Club, 529 14th St NW). EFF's first office was at 155 Second Street, Cambridge, Massachusetts, per Barlow's November 1990 'A Not Terribly Brief History of the Electronic Frontier Foundation' (eff.org).

issues: The summary says 'led a court to hold that e-mail deserves at least as much protection as telephone calls' as if it were the court's holding. That wording is EFF's own gloss from its history page. The actual 12 March 1993 ruling by Judge Sam Sparks (W.D. Tex.) awarded each plaintiff $1,000 under the ECPA for the seizure of their stored e-mail, but 'did not find that Secret Service agents had "intercepted" the electronic communications' (EFFector 5/4, 19 March 1993). The Fifth Circuit upheld that no-interception finding in October 1994, which is the opposite of telephone-call-level (Wiretap Act) protection. The sentence is reworded to state the real holding and attribute the gloss to EFF.

'EFF's first case' is EFF's own label (eff.org/issues/video-games: 'EFF's first case in 1990...'). Barlow's 8 November 1990 history, however, shows EFF's first legal action was a supporting amicus brief for Craig Neidorf, whose prosecution collapsed in late July 1990. The Steve Jackson Games suit was the lawsuit announced at launch. The wording is changed to 'the lawsuit EFF announced at its launch'.

The significance field claims EFF was 'the first advocacy organisation built to argue for privacy and speech rights inside networks'. That is overstated. Barlow's 1990 history records that one of EFF's first acts was a $275,000 grant to Computer Professionals for Social Responsibility's existing Washington office 'for a project on computing and civil liberties'. 'the first' is dropped.

The other claims check out: 1 March 1990 raid (SSIR), stored BBS e-mail 'individually accessed and deleted' (EFF history), the Kapor/Barlow/Gilmore founders, the 10 July 1990 National Press Club announcement (SSIR and Barlow 1990: 'We announced the formation of the Electronic Frontier Foundation at the National Press Club on July 10'), and the founding-paper quote. The locationNote's '155 Second St. Cambridge, MA 02141' is FOUND in Barlow's 8 November 1990 history.

events.title: Barlow's 'Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace'
events.place: Davos, Switzerland (World Economic Forum annual meeting)
events.summary: On 8 February 1996, the day President Clinton signed the Telecommunications Act of 1996 with its Communications Decency Act, John Perry Barlow wrote a manifesto at the close of the World Economic Forum in Davos telling 'Governments of the Industrial World' they had no sovereignty online. He e-mailed it to about 600 friends the next day; by his count it was on at least 10,000 websites within a month. Twenty years later Barlow stood by it while conceding that online self-regulation had in most ways not developed.
events.significance: A founding text of the claim that people online could set their own rules, the libertarian starting point that later privacy advocates both built on and argued against.

sources.title: John Perry Barlow, 'A Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace'
sources.quote: In the United States, you have today created a law, the Telecommunications Reform Act, which repudiates your own Constitution and insults the dreams of Jefferson, Washington, Mill, Madison, DeToqueville, and Brandeis.
sources.note: Signed 'Davos, Switzerland February 8, 1996'.

sources.note: The same text says he wrote it at 'a staff party for the closing of the World Economic Forum' and sent it 'the next day to the 600 or so friends I had with e-mail addresses'.

None of the sources establish that superlative, and cyberspace-autonomy arguments were already circulating, for example in EFF's own 1990 'Across the Electronic Frontier'. It is changed to 'A founding text'. Every factual claim in the summary checked out.

events.title: The first DEF CON puts hackers, lawyers and a prosecutor in one room
events.place: Sands Hotel & Casino, Las Vegas, Nevada
events.summary: Jeff Moss ('The Dark Tangent'), organising from Seattle, turned a farewell party for a bulletin-board friend into a convention, inviting 'hackers/phreaks, techno-rats, programmers, writers, activists, lawyers, philosophers, politicians, security officials' to the Sands Hotel, Las Vegas, on Friday to Sunday 9–11 July 1993, at $30 at the door. InfoWorld's Robert X. Cringely reported that the Operation Sun Devil prosecutor spoke and told the young crowd 'I'm not here to bust you'. Billed as the '1st annual Def Con', it grew into a gathering that The Record put at some 30,000 hackers in 2025.
events.significance: Created a standing meeting ground where hackers, security staff, lawyers and law enforcement argue in public over surveillance, security and privacy.

Also FOUND: 'DEF CON I will be over the weekend in the middle of down town Las Vegas at the Sands Hotel.' and the invitation list quoted in the summary. 9 July 1993 was a Friday. DEF CON's own archive page (https://defcon.org/html/links/dc-archives/dc-1-archive.html) says 'Was June 9-11, 1993' — see myth record.

events.title: Hackers On Planet Earth: 2600's first HOPE conference
events.place: Hotel Pennsylvania, Manhattan, New York City
events.summary: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly marked its tenth anniversary with Hackers On Planet Earth, held at the Hotel Pennsylvania in Manhattan on 13–14 August 1994 and attended by well over 1,000 people. Inspired by the Dutch hacker gatherings of the 1980s and 1990s, it was, by its organisers' account, the first hacker conference of that size attempted in the United States, with talks 'ranging from privacy issues to technology to politics' and a 'Cryptography and Privacy' session featuring Eric Hughes and Matt Blaze. HOPE became a recurring New York conference, annual from 2025.
events.significance: Gave the hacker scene around 2600 a large public forum in New York where surveillance, cryptography and privacy were argued before a mass audience.

sources.title: Hackers On Planet Earth
sources.quote: Hackers On Planet Earth, a conference in New York City, marking 2600 Magazine's 10 year anniversary, took place on August 13th-14th of 1994.
sources.note: Also FOUND: 'Well over 1000 people were in attendance at this gala event.' and 'Speakers from around the world made presentations ranging from privacy issues to technology to politics to methodologies.'

sources.title: About HOPE
sources.quote: The first Hackers On Planet Earth (HOPE) conference took place at the Hotel Pennsylvania in Manhattan, New York City over two days.
sources.note: Same page: 'It was the first time that a hacker conference of this size had been attempted in the United States and it was inspired by the Dutch hacker gatherings of the 80s and 90s.' and 'In 2025, for the first time ever, HOPE became an annual event.' The 2600 store lists a 1994 recording titled 'Cryptography and Privacy' (https://store.2600.com/collections/hackers-on-planet-earth).

sources.title: Hackers On Planet Earth (1994): "Cryptography and Privacy" (Download)
sources.quote: Saturday, August 13, 1994, 10:00 pm: There have been quite a few articles in the national media recently about cryptography and privacy.
sources.note: --check FOUND. The same listing is FOUND saying 'Also featuring Eric Hughes and Matt Blaze.' It also describes Bob Stratton's introduction and a demonstration of 'the AT&T 3600 Surety device, the world's first Clipper Chip telephone encryption unit'.

events.locationNote: Hotel Pennsylvania, Seventh Avenue, Manhattan — HOPE's usual venue until The Circle of HOPE, the last HOPE held there (per hope.net/about).

issues: Summary calls the 1994 cryptography item 'a panel on cryptography and privacy'. The 2600 store listing shows it was a session titled 'Cryptography and Privacy' introduced by Bob Stratton, with a Clipper Chip (AT&T 3600 Surety) demonstration by Bernie S. and John Turbo and also featuring Eric Hughes and Matt Blaze. 2600 titles its real panels explicitly ('The 2600 Panel', 'The Author Panel', 'The Cellular Panel'), and this one is not billed as a panel. The wording is changed to 'session'. The Clipper demonstration is left out of the summary because the listing is a programme description written in the future tense ('will attempt').
'Modelled on the Dutch hacker gatherings' overstates the source, which says only 'inspired by'.

'the first US hacker conference on that scale' is HOPE's own claim ('the first time that a hacker conference of this size had been attempted in the United States'). The summary now attributes it to the organisers.

Dates (13-14 August 1994), venue (Hotel Pennsylvania), attendance (well over 1,000), 2600's tenth anniversary and 'annual from 2025' are all confirmed on the cited pages. Wikipedia independently gives 'August 13-14, 1994', 'Over 1,000 people attended'.

events.title: Aaron Swartz's DeadDrop becomes SecureDrop
events.place: Freedom of the Press Foundation, San Francisco, California
events.summary: Four months after the first Snowden stories, the Freedom of the Press Foundation announced on 15 October 2013 that it had taken over DeadDrop, the whistleblower-submission system coded by Aaron Swartz in partnership with the journalist Kevin Poulsen, who managed the project, renamed it SecureDrop and would install it in newsrooms. Each source receives a codename so they can keep talking to a newsroom without revealing their identity or using e-mail. The code had been audited by University of Washington researchers; The New Yorker, the first user since May 2013 under the name Strongbox, was to keep running its installation.
events.significance: Made source anonymity a standard, shareable piece of newsroom infrastructure — privacy enforced by system design rather than by a publisher's promise.

sources.quote: Each source who uses the platform is assigned a unique codename that lets the source establish a relationship with the news organization without having to reveal her real identity or resort to e-mail.
sources.note: Dateline FOUND: 'October 15, 2013 San Francisco, CA : Freedom of the Press Foundation has taken charge of the DeadDrop project'. Also FOUND: the University of Washington audit sentence, and that 'The New Yorker, the first news organization to use the SecureDrop code, through its StrongBox project , will continue to operate its system.'

sources.title: Kevin Poulsen, 'Strongbox and Aaron Swartz'
sources.quote: The New Yorker ’ s version is called Strongbox; it went online this morning .
sources.note: The spacing reproduces the page text as extracted.

sources.title: SecureDrop FAQ
sources.quote: Investigative journalist Kevin Poulsen originally managed the project. The New Yorker launched the first implementation and branded their version StrongBox in May 2013.
sources.note: --check FOUND. The same page is FOUND saying 'The web application, which was originally called DeadDrop, was developed by Aaron Swartz in 2012 before his tragic death.'

events.locationNote: Dateline of the announcement: San Francisco, California (city centroid).

issues: 'coded by Aaron Swartz with Kevin Poulsen' suggests Poulsen co-wrote the code. The FPF release says the system was 'originally coded by the late transparency advocate Aaron Swartz' and 'created by Swartz in partnership with investigative reporter Kevin Poulsen'. SecureDrop's own FAQ says it was 'developed by Aaron Swartz' and that 'Kevin Poulsen originally managed the project'. The summary is reworded so that Swartz wrote it and Poulsen partnered on and managed it.

'kept its installation' is correct for October 2013 (FPF: 'will continue to operate its system'). However, the New Yorker article now carries 'Update: The New Yorker is no longer using Strongbox.' The summary is reworded so readers do not take this as still true.

Checked and correct: date 15 October 2013 and San Francisco dateline, rename to SecureDrop, codename mechanism, University of Washington audit (led by Alexei Czeskis), New Yorker Strongbox launch on 14 May 2013 (page datePublished 2013-05-14), and 'four months after the first Snowden stories' (June 2013).

events.title: Max Schrems founds noyb to enforce the GDPR against companies
events.summary: noyb ('none of your business'), the European Center for Digital Rights, was founded in Vienna on 12 June 2017 by Max Schrems, who had brought down the EU–US Safe Harbour framework. Crowdfunded towards a €500,000 target, it set out to focus on commercial privacy violations and to use GDPR Article 80 to bring collective complaints; it became operational on 1 February 2018 and filed its first cases on 25 May 2018, the GDPR's first day, against 'forced consent' at Google, Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram.
events.significance: Created a standing enforcer that turns individuals' GDPR rights into collective action against platforms — the institutional counterpart to people asserting their own terms.

events.title: The Wall Street Journal's 'What They Know' counts the trackers
events.place: The Wall Street Journal newsroom, Midtown Manhattan, New York City
events.summary: On 30 July 2010 The Wall Street Journal opened 'What They Know', an investigation led by Julia Angwin with technical consultant Ashkan Soltani, with 'The Web's New Gold Mine: Your Secrets'. Testing the 50 most popular US websites, the Journal found they installed an average of 64 pieces of tracking technology — cookies, Flash cookies and beacons — on a visitor's computer, usually with no warning. Later instalments covered mobile apps, device fingerprinting and how Microsoft's advertising side blocked stronger privacy features planned for Internet Explorer 8.
events.significance: Measured the third-party tracking economy for a mass audience and fed Congressional and FTC efforts to rein in the tracking industry.

The compilation's table of contents lists later instalments including 'Microsoft Quashed Effort To Boost Online Privacy', 'Race Is On To ‘Fingerprint’ Phones, PCs' and 'Your Apps Are Watching You'. Original: wsj.com (paywalled).

events.title: Kashmir Hill exposes Clearview AI's scraped face database
events.place: The New York Times newsroom, Manhattan, New York City
events.summary: The New York Times article 'The Secretive Company That Might End Privacy as We Know It' by Kashmir Hill, dated 18 January 2020 in its web address, revealed that the start-up Clearview AI had built a face-search app on a database of more than three billion images it claimed to have scraped from Facebook, YouTube, Venmo and millions of other websites, and that — according to the company — more than 600 law-enforcement agencies had started using it in the past year. After the story, New Jersey's attorney general barred the state's police from using it, Vermont's attorney general sued and members of Congress demanded answers; Australia's privacy regulator opened inquiries on 21 January 2020 and in October 2021 ordered the company to stop collecting and to destroy Australians' images.
events.significance: Showed that anything a person posts can be harvested into a biometric identification system without consent — and that after-the-fact 'opt-out' forms are no substitute for terms set before collection.

sources.title: EPIC FOIA request to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Clearview AI (6 March 2020)
sources.quote: Clearview has scraped more than 3 billion images from websites and social media platforms such as Facebook, YouTube, Venmo, and Twitter.
sources.note: Also FOUND: 'Within the past year, more than 600 law enforcement agencies have started using the Clearview AI app.' Both sentences are footnoted to the Times article, cited as 'Kashmir Hill, The Secretive Company That Might End Privacy as We Know It, N.Y. Times (Feb. 10, 2020), https://www.nytimes.com/2020/01/18/technology/clearview-privacy-facial-recognition.html' (the Feb. 10 date is a later update; the URL carries the 18 January 2020 original). The Times page itself blocks scripted access (403/JS wall) and was not read.

sources.title: ACLU Sues Clearview AI (press release)
sources.quote: Following the NYT story, the New Jersey attorney general prohibited state law enforcement from using Clearview’s system, the Vermont attorney general sued, and members of Congress demanded answers.
sources.note: Also FOUND: 'Clearview gained national attention after the New York Times revealed the company was secretly capturing untold numbers of biometric identifiers for purposes of surveillance and tracking, without notice to the individuals affected.' The ACLU is a party to litigation against Clearview.

sources.institution: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
sources.title: Commissioner initiated investigation into Clearview AI, Inc. (Privacy) [2021] AICmr 54 (14 October 2021)
sources.quote: On 21 January 2020, the OAIC sent preliminary inquiries to the respondent
sources.note: The determination orders that Clearview 'must cease to collect Scraped Images, Probe Images, Scraped Image Vectors, Probe Image Vectors and Opt-out Vectors' from individuals in Australia and destroy those held; it records that 'From 29 January 2020, it began to offer Australian residents an online form to ‘opt-out’' which later 'became no longer accessible'.

sources.institution: Gulf News (syndicated The New York Times article)
sources.title: The secretive company that might end privacy as we know it
sources.quote: The system - whose backbone is a database of more than 3 billion images that Clearview claims to have scraped from Facebook, YouTube, Venmo and millions of other websites - goes far beyond anything ever constructed by the US government or Silicon Valley giants.
sources.note: --check FOUND. Page JSON-LD: author 'NYT', datePublished 2020-01-19T21:12:08+04:00. This is the Times text syndicated, since the original nytimes.com page blocks scripted access. Also FOUND: 'But without public scrutiny, more than 600 law enforcement agencies have started using Clearview in the past year, according to the company, which declined to provide a list.'

events.locationNote: Approximate coordinates of the Times building in Midtown Manhattan. The ACLU describes Clearview as 'a little-known start-up based in New York' (https://www.aclu.org/news/privacy-technology/were-taking-clearview-ai-to-court-to-end-its-privacy-destroying-face-surveillance-activities).

issues: The summary says the Times 'revealed that the start-up Clearview AI had scraped more than three billion images from Facebook, YouTube, Venmo, Twitter and other sites'. The original article, read via Gulf News's syndicated copy of the NYT text dated 19 January 2020, hedges this: 'a database of more than 3 billion images that Clearview claims to have scraped from Facebook, YouTube, Venmo and millions of other websites'. Twitter does not appear anywhere in that text. It comes from EPIC's paraphrase, which cites the Times article's 10 February 2020 update.

The '600 agencies' figure was the company's own claim and was not independently verified: 'more than 600 law enforcement agencies have started using Clearview in the past year, according to the company, which declined to provide a list.'

'New Jersey's attorney general barred state police from using it' is too narrow and ambiguous, since it can be read as the New Jersey State Police only. The ACLU says the AG 'prohibited state law enforcement from using Clearview’s system'. EPIC says New Jersey 'banned statewide law enforcement agencies', and the NYT follow-up is headlined 'New Jersey Bars Police From Using Clearview Facial Recognition App'.

Checked and correct: Vermont AG lawsuit and congressional demands (ACLU), OAIC preliminary inquiries on 21 January 2020, and the October 2021 cease-collection and destroy orders. The OAIC determination is cited as [2021] AICmr 54 (14 October 2021), but the PDF's signature block reads '22 October 2021'. Either way 'October 2021' holds.

myths.claim: The first DEF CON was held on 9–11 June 1993.
myths.correction: The June date appears on DEF CON's own archive page and is widely repeated, but the organisers' finalized announcement, dated 12 June 1993, gives 'July 9th, 10th and 11th (Fri, Sat, Sun) 1993' — 9 July 1993 was a Friday — and InfoWorld's issue of 19 July 1993 described DEF CON I as 'last week in Las Vegas'. myths.claim: In 1984 Chaos Computer Club hackers robbed a Hamburg savings bank of about DM 135,000.
myths.correction: The 'bank robbery' was a demonstration. On the night of 16–17 November 1984, using the Hamburger Sparkasse's Btx login, a small program called up a CCC page priced at DM 9.97 about 13,500 times. That ran up a virtual DM 134,694.70 (the figure on the Bundespost's own 1985 statement; heise gives DM 134,634.88) that 'theoretically went to the CCC'. The club had warned the Bundespost and data-protection officials in October 1984. On Monday 19 November it demonstrated the hack at the Hamburg data-protection commissioner's office, told the press, made no claim to the money and called for a ban on financial transactions on Btx.

myths.claim: Wau Holland founded the Chaos Computer Club.
myths.correction: Holland was a co-founder and the club's best-known voice, but the taz notice of 1 September 1981 that called the founding meeting was signed by five Hamburg men — Klaus Schleisiek ('Tom Twiddlebit'), Wau Holland, Wolf Gevert and two unnamed others later identified as Wulf Müller and Jochen Büttner — and about 20 people attended the 12 September 1981 meeting in Berlin.

sources.note: Translation: 'Behind the pseudonym Tom Twiddlebit was Klaus Schleisiek; Wau stood for Herwart Holland-Moritz, known as Wau Holland; Wolf meant Wolf Gevert.' The thesis continues: 'Die zwei Ungenannten waren Wulf Müller und Jochen Büttner' and 'Zu dem Treffen sollen etwa 20 Personen gekommen sein' (both FOUND).

sources.title: Chaos Computer Club – Club (Selbstdarstellung)
sources.quote: Das Treffen führte zunächst zu einer informellen Gründung des Chaos Computer Clubs und wurde als regelmäßiger Treff in Hamburg weitergeführt.
sources.note: Independent check from the club's own self-description (undated web page). Translation: 'The meeting first led to an informal founding of the Chaos Computer Club and was continued as a regular meet-up in Hamburg.' The previous sentence is also FOUND: 'Am Tisch der Kommune 1 der Zeitung taz in Berlin trafen sich damals Hacker, selbstbezeichnete „Komputerfrieks“ im Rahmen des „tu-wat“-Kongresses.' It shows a group meeting, not one founder.

sources.quote: the doyen and co-founder of the Chaos Computer Club throughout several decades until his untimely death on July 29, 2001
sources.note: Even the foundation set up in his memory calls him 'co-founder'. The same page also says 'Through founding the Chaos Computer Club in 1981, Wau Holland paved the way...', which shows how the shorthand in this myth arises.

issues: No factual error found. Every element of the correction matches Röhr's thesis (pp. 58-60): the taz 'TUWAT,TXT' notice of 1 September 1981 (footnote 319: taz, 01. September 1981, S. 2), the meeting called for 12.9.81 at the taz building in Berlin (Wattstr.), the signature 'Tom Twiddlebit, Wau Wolf Ungenannt(»2)', the names Schleisiek, Holland-Moritz, Gevert, Müller and Büttner, and 'die fünf einladenden Hamburger'.

Minor hedge: the thesis reports the attendance as hearsay ('sollen etwa 20 Personen gekommen sein' = 'about 20 people are said to have come'). The correction's 'about 20 people attended' is acceptable and needs no change.

Verdict MISLEADING (rather than FALSE) is right. The CCC itself calls the 1981 meeting only an 'informelle Gründung'. The Wau Holland Foundation calls him 'doyen and co-founder', though the same page also says 'Through founding the Chaos Computer Club in 1981, Wau Holland...', which is the sole-founder shorthand this myth corrects. Röhr also records that the club set up its registered association (e.V.) only in spring 1986 ('gründete der Club im Frühjahr 1986 einen eingetragenen Verein').

myths.claim: John Perry Barlow delivered 'A Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace' as a speech to world leaders at the Davos World Economic Forum.
myths.correction: Barlow wrote the text at Davos but not as a speech: by his own account he wrote it during a party at the close of the 1996 World Economic Forum, as a contribution to the book 24 Hours in Cyberspace (whose editors found it too controversial to use), and e-mailed it the next day to about 600 friends, from where it spread online.

issues: The claim, verdict (MISLEADING) and correction all hold. Barlow's own 2016 account says he wrote the piece at 'a staff party for the closing of the World Economic Forum', for the book 24 Hours in Cyberspace, whose editors 'found it too controversial to include'. It also says he 'sent it out the next day to the 600 or so friends I had with e-mail addresses'. Wired (Andy Greenberg, 2016-02-08) confirms the story independently: it was written at a party on the last night of the 1996 WEF in Davos, 'in one of the hotel's side rooms', as a contribution to '24 Hours In Cyberspace'. EFF's canonical text carries the dateline 'Davos, Switzerland February 8, 1996'. Nothing shows it was ever delivered as a speech.

Minor, in source 1 only: the note on the Doctorow source calls it 'the accurate framing'. But Doctorow's phrase 'where he'd been addressing world leaders' is not supported by Barlow's own account (he says WEF brought in wired types 'mostly as curiosities') or by Wired (he 'spent the previous four days in Davos listening ... to world leaders'). The Doctorow line is better presented as a secondary account that already leans toward the 'speaking to world leaders' framing, while still describing a written document. The note is corrected below; the record's fields need no change.
